description:
We are a team of two members passionate about satellite technology, Earth observation, remote sensing, and environmental data analysis.

Our project, sensorSinergy, focuses on exploring MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors and their applications in monitoring our planet. We aim to understand how satellite data can help identify environmental changes, monitor vegetation, detect wildfires, and analyze climate and land surface conditions.

Our team combines curiosity, research.
summary:
sensorSinergy is a web-based platform designed to harmonize historical active fire hotspot data from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors. It addresses the challenge of comparing fire activity records from different satellite missions, whose observations vary in spatial resolution, sensitivity, and coverage.

By integrating and processing these datasets, the project aims to provide a consistent view of global fire activity over time. Users can explore hotspot distribution across selected regions and periods, identify seasonal patterns, compare activity between years, and detect unusual changes against historical baselines.

The platform combines geospatial visualization, historical analysis, and an interactive burning activity calendar to make satellite-derived information easier to understand and use. Its goal is to support early warning, scientific research, land management, and emergency response through more accessible and consistent information about fire activity.
details:
sensorSinergy – Sense. Analyze. Act. is a project focused on developing a global historical fire activity monitoring platform using satellite-derived active fire hotspot data.

The project addresses the challenge of combining MODIS and VIIRS observations into a more consistent dataset. Since these sensors have different spatial resolutions, detection capabilities, and observation characteristics, their records require careful processing and harmonization before meaningful historical comparisons can be made.

The proposed solution follows two main stages. First, hotspot data from NASA FIRMS are collected, validated, organized, and processed while preserving their original sensor information. The harmonized dataset is then used as the basis for the web application.

The application is designed to allow users to explore fire activity through an interactive map, select geographic areas and date ranges, consult a burning activity calendar, compare historical patterns, identify unusual variations, and export hotspot records in CSV format.

The project aims to make historical fire information more accessible and useful to emergency responders, scientists, land managers, and other users involved in fire monitoring and risk management.

The proposed technical architecture includes Python for data processing, PostgreSQL with PostGIS for geospatial storage, FastAPI for data services, and React/Next.js with Leaflet for the web interface.

Its main contribution is the integration of long-term satellite observations into a common analytical environment, helping users understand seasonal fire patterns and changes in burning activity over time.
